### UTC Date & Time

[November 16, 2026, 14:00 UTC](https://savvytime.com/converter/utc/nov-16-2026/2pm)

### Agenda

#### Glamsterdam

##### EIP-8037/8038: Compatibility Investigations & Audit Findings

The goal is to establish a shared understanding of the current findings, their impact on deployed contracts, and any remaining uncertainties. This discussion will help inform the next steps at Thursday's ACDE https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/2285.

###### Resources

- [Vitalik's views on EIP-8037](https://docs.fileverse.io/document/dUHG8ythBk3jJuQEjcE7m6#k=tVLgvLrIqyEsCh7qUmACb9ggVmybyS_aIZZsAMvHDAk).
- Ethereum Foundation [blog post](https://blog.ethereum.org/2026/11/06/glamsterdam-8037-8038).
- EthLabs [blog post](https://ethlabs.org/writings/tracking-glamsterdam.html).
- Repository outlining the potentially changed gas invariants: [ethereum/glamsterdam-gas-invariants](https://github.com/ethereum/glamsterdam-gas-invariants).
- EVM Gas Repricing analysis: [misilva73/evm-gas-repricings](https://github.com/misilva73/evm-gas-repricings).
- Initial ChainSecurity report: [Presentation at ACDE #248](https://forkcast.org/calls/acde/248/#t=304), [blog post](https://www.chainsecurity.com/blog/glamsterdam-gas/index.html).

###### 8037/8038 agenda

- **Overview and current status:** @MariusVanDerWijden
- **Independent audit findings:**
  - [ChainSecurity](https://www.chainsecurity.com/): @TanguyRocher-ChainSecurity
  - [Dedaub](https://dedaub.com/): @Dedaub
- **EF internal investigations:** @nerolation, Architecture, EF
- **Application team outreach and contract findings:** @rahul-kothari, EVM Dev Tooling, EF
  - Juicebox protocol compatibility concerns and PoCs, @mejango, resp. @rahul-kothari , ([comment](https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/2299#issuecomment-6860064283)).
    - Details: [mejango/glamsterdam-pocs](https://github.com/mejango/glamsterdam-pocs).
- **Open Q&A:** Audit findings, affected contracts, outstanding concerns, and input from application developers
- **Ethereum can better align the app layer and protocol layer moving forward**
  - EF Access Layer cluster is a new group within the EF to help address these issues @rahul-kothari.
  - The core EIP process will more tightly coupled to the app layer @marioevz 
    - Examples:
      - [ethereum/execution-specs#3948 feat(tests): add a deployed-idiom invariant corpus](https://github.com/ethereum/execution-specs/pull/3948).
      - [ethereum/execution-specs#3982 feat(test-specs): check chain invariants while filling](https://github.com/ethereum/execution-specs/pull/3982).
  - New EIP documenting the scope of invariants that could break, avoid these anti-patterns in smart contracts @nerolation.
  
##### Payload Binding: Select a Solution

Follow-up from ACDC. Discuss the two proposed solutions and decide which to adopt to unblock the consensus spec release @jtraglia ([comment](https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/2299#issuecomment-6831513586)):
- https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/pull/5770
- https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/pull/5820

##### Heads up

- Please participate in the EIPIP call on Wednesday: https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/2288#issuecomment-6845904473 to discuss AI usage in the EIP process by @jochem-brouwer ([comment](https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/2299#issuecomment-6893348620)).

my 2 cents re the eip-8037 & eip-8038 discussion

---

**ethereum's social contract: immutability requires predictable execution**

ethereum's value proposition is not simply that anyone can deploy _immutable_ smart contracts. it is that anyone can build systems whose guarantees do _not_ depend on trusting an intermediary, an administrator, or a governance process. the discussion around eip-8037 & eip-8038 exposes a fundamental problem with how we approach protocol changes. ethereum needs to scale (for me personally this is not a top priority but i accept that this is a clear user demand). repricing resources may be necessary. but there is a fundamental difference between changing the price of an operation and changing the behavioural assumptions applications have been built around.

the [glamsterdam gas invariants](https://github.com/ethereum/glamsterdam-gas-invariants) document _eight_ assumptions affected by these eips. some concern gas repricing; others concern execution & accounting semantics, including gas refunds, nested calls, reverts and `gasleft()`. these are not merely implementation details. they can affect control flow, failure handling & security assumptions in deployed applications. now the concerning part is that these implications were **not** systematically captured as **first-class invariants** in the specification and validation process early enough. some warnings existed earlier (see e.g. [here](https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/eip-8037-state-creation-gas-cost-increase/25694/30)), but the broader implications only became the subject of a structured review very late in the process (~3 weeks ago).

**we should not be discovering protocol-level behavioural invariants retrospectively, weeks before a major upgrade.**

there is also an assumption worth challenging: that gas schedules must necessarily remain mutable for existing contracts. **predictability is itself a protocol property**. changing execution economics underneath immutable contracts can effectively change their behaviour without changing a single byte of their code. we should distinguish economic repricing from changes to execution semantics, and explicitly consider whether existing contracts should retain their original execution guarantees. immutability without predictable execution is _incomplete_. removing upgrade keys & admin privileges at the application layer means little if protocol changes can silently invalidate the security properties those applications rely on.

this is _not_ an argument against protocol evolution. it is an argument for a higher burden of proof when breaking established behavioural assumptions.

**how we can do better, some thoughts**

- **formalise invariants:** document behavioural guarantees and distinguish them from implementation details and economic parameters.
- **incorporate them into specifications:** explicitly identify which invariants an eip preserves, changes, or introduces.
- **test them continuously:** introduce adversarial, invariant-based regression tests covering nested calls, reverts, refunds, out-of-gas conditions, and gas boundaries.
- **test deployed applications:** evaluate protocol changes against real-world immutable contracts and their composability assumptions.
- **make compatibility explicit:** document breaking changes, migration requirements, and possible backwards-compatibility mechanisms before finalising eips.

**we should not confuse consensus compatibility with application compatibility**. a hard fork can be perfectly deterministic and consistently implemented across clients while still breaking deployed applications.

ethereum's long-term value is not determined exclusively by throughput, gas limits, or execution efficiency. it also depends on whether people can build systems that remain trustworthy without continually renegotiating their assumptions with whoever governs the protocol.

**we can do better. we must do better.**

As mentioned, I can discuss the gas refills topic:

EIP-8037 charges the full account creation cost of 183,600 state gas to a contract that is created and self-destructed in the same transaction, even though no account, code or storage is left behind. The create itself goes from 32,000 gas today to about 195,600, roughly 6x. Whole transactions that use the pattern go up 1.6x to 2.8x in our measurements.

This pattern is in production for temporary deposit addresses and other short-lived execution flows, and more than one company depends on it. On Ethereum mainnet we count about 2,100 such contracts per day (6 November 2026), up from about 1,200 per day in August.

On other EVMs this is 10x more. 

The operators include many companies, from payments to bridge aggregators. 

The original EIP-8037 text refilled this state gas at the end of the transaction. That section was removed in PR #11611 in May 2026 without a stated reason, and the proposal to restore it (PR #12249) was closed. I would ask that the refill for contracts created and destroyed within the same transaction is reconsidered, or at least that this impact is evaluated explicitly before the fork is finalized. TCREATE (EIP-8360) is not in Glamsterdam and is not a drop-in replacement for the addresses already issued.

cc @rahul-kothari

So, instead of lying to ourselves, let's say it how it is. There is a compromise to be made, or rather a decision. A. You become/merge into a zk first primitives stateless ledger. B. You keep the state bloating up, price out solo/indie. (with the perspective of TradFi taking over and purging state)
